speaker_role: student (Stanford undergraduate reviewing his own admissions file)
key_insights: Describes the FERPA process for requesting to view one's own admissions file; his virtual session was read aloud to him in a 20-minute slot with no electronics allowed, only handwritten notes.

His file reportedly showed rating codes RTG (testing), HSR (high school rigor), SUP (support/recommendation letters), EC (extracurriculars), and SPIV (self-presentation/intellectual vitality), each on what he infers is a 1(best)-5 scale from crowd-sourced online research.
His two application readers gave him identical sub-scores (3s) on HSR/SUP/EC/SPIV but differing overall evaluation ratings (2- and 3+), a discrepancy he could not explain.

Interview ratings used a separate inferred 1-6 scale (1 best); he scored 3/2/3 across intellectual vitality, depth & commitment, and character/self-presentation, which he interprets as a solid interview.
One reader's written summary described his application as 'not jumping off the page' and 'on the fence,' while also noting his intended major worked in his favor.

Concludes that despite non-standout reader comments/scores, something happened between the initial reads and the final committee vote that tipped the decision in his favor, which he could not identify.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Reader sub-scores of 3 on HSR/SUP/EC/SPIV categories (inferred 1-5 scale, per applicant's own research)
Overall evaluation ratings of 2- and 3+ from his two readers
Interview ratings of 3/2/3 on a stated 1-6 scale
notable_or_distinctive: A firsthand, if redacted and note-taken, look at literal Stanford admissions-file rating-code abbreviations (RTG, HSR, SUP, EC, SPIV) and how reader scores and interview scores can diverge from the final committee decision.
reliability_notes: The meanings of the rating-code abbreviations are the applicant's own speculation/crowd-sourced guesses ('from what I've read online'), not confirmed by Stanford; notes were transcribed from a read-aloud session so details may be incomplete or imperfectly captured; this is a single anecdote, not representative of general policy, presented in a casual vlog format.
